data.title: Top 10 DC Fast Charger Manufacturers in China (2026): Global Buyer’s Guide
data.description: Compare 10 DC fast charger manufacturers in China and see their main strengths, product focus and suitable project applications.
data.content:
China has a large and diverse EV charging manufacturing sector. For global buyers, that creates plenty of choice—but also makes supplier selection more complicated.

Different DC fast charger manufacturers focus on different areas. Some have strong high-power distributed charging systems, while others place more emphasis on integrated chargers, software, international standards or OEM customization.

The following 10 manufacturers are presented in no particular order. This is not a ranking by sales, market share or product quality. Instead, it is a practical starting point for buyers comparing DC charging suppliers in China in 2026.


10 DC Fast Charger Manufacturers in China to Consider

StarCharge

StarCharge offers both integrated and split DC charging systems. Its current public portfolio includes smaller dual-connector chargers as well as 360kW, 480kW and higher-power distributed systems. Some models are designed for highway, public parking and depot applications.

For buyers evaluating larger charging networks or a broad charger portfolio, StarCharge is one manufacturer worth including in the initial comparison.


Sinexcel

Sinexcel has a strong background in power electronics and offers both charging modules and complete EV charging equipment.

Its 480kW distributed charging system supports OCPP 1.6J and OCPP 2.0 and lists several international certification options for different markets.

This may make Sinexcel relevant for buyers working on high-power projects where backend integration and regional compliance are important selection criteria.


Autel Energy

Autel Energy has expanded its commercial DC charging range from compact units to higher-power systems. Its current portfolio includes a 40kW compact charger, 60–240kW products, the 120–480kW DH480 and a 640kW high-power system.

Autel may be worth evaluating for projects where charging hardware, software and energy-management functions are expected to work as part of one ecosystem.


Grasen

Grasen manufactures integrated and distributed DC fast charging equipment for commercial and public charging projects.

Its product range includes compact DC chargers, 60–480kW integrated units with single-, dual-, triple- or four-connector configurations, as well as distributed charging systems reaching up to 3200kW and 24 charging connectors. Products support CCS, CHAdeMO, GB/T and NACS configurations, together with OCPP connectivity and remote management functions.

Grasen may suit distributors, charging operators and project developers looking for flexible power, connector and software configurations for different charging-site requirements.


TELD

TELD approaches EV charging from both the equipment and charging-network side.

Its product portfolio includes integrated DC chargers, European-standard 60–160kW chargers, liquid-cooled terminals and group-charging systems, together with charging operation and safety-management platforms.

TELD is therefore more relevant to buyers interested in large charging networks and centralized charging infrastructure than to those simply sourcing an individual charger model.


BENY

BENY combines EV charging equipment with solar and electrical products.

Its DC range includes single-, dual- and multi-connector chargers, with public models covering power levels up to 240kW and beyond. Some products support CCS1, CCS2, CHAdeMO, GB/T and NACS configurations, as well as OCPP and multiple network connections.

It may be useful to evaluate BENY where EV charging is being sourced alongside broader renewable-energy or electrical equipment.


EN Plus

EN Plus offers AC and DC charging equipment as well as a charging-operation platform.

Its public DC portfolio ranges from smaller DC chargers to 240kW integrated units, 320–500kW heavy-duty chargers and 480–960kW distributed charging systems.

For buyers comparing both charging hardware and operator-management functions, EN Plus provides a relatively broad range of options to assess.


SETEC Power

SETEC Power focuses on DC charging equipment and customized charging applications.

The company states that its chargers support OCPP 1.6 JSON and OCPP 2.0.1, and it offers OEM/ODM customization for areas such as appearance, branding and platform integration.

This may make SETEC worth considering for buyers with non-standard project requirements or those who place a higher priority on customization.


Winline

Winline has a strong power-electronics focus and offers charging modules as well as high-power distributed charging systems.

Its public split-charger portfolio includes 360kW, 480kW, 720kW and 960kW systems, with various terminal and cooling configurations available depending on the platform.

Winline is particularly relevant when evaluating high-power charging hubs where modular power distribution is a major part of the project design.


SCU

SCU provides both integrated charging equipment and centralized power-cabinet plus dispenser systems.

Its current split DC charging range includes 480kW, 640kW and 960kW platforms, with support for several connector standards and intelligent power allocation.

It may be worth comparing for fleet, public charging or larger multi-dispenser projects where system scalability is important.


What Should Buyers Compare Before Choosing a DC Fast Charger Manufacturer?

A manufacturer with the highest power rating is not automatically the best choice for every project.

Global buyers should first check whether the supplier can meet the requirements of the specific destination market and charging site.

Key points include:

· Power range: Does the supplier cover the power required today and possible future expansion?

· Connector standards: Confirm CCS1, CCS2, CHAdeMO, GB/T, NACS or other required interfaces.

· OCPP and software: Check the required OCPP version and compatibility with your CSMS.

· Certification: Verify certification for the actual model and destination market rather than relying on general company claims.

· Customization: Consider connector combinations, branding, payment terminals, software and communication requirements.

· Service and spare parts: Ask how faults, firmware updates, warranty issues and replacement parts are handled after deployment.

These questions are often more useful than comparing product brochures line by line.


Why the Lowest Charger Price Is Not Always the Best Deal

Price matters, especially for larger orders, but the charger itself is only one part of a commercial charging project.

A lower quotation can lose its advantage if the equipment creates problems with software integration, spare parts, maintenance or market compliance later.

For that reason, buyers comparing EV DC fast charger manufacturers should look at the supplier's overall ability to support the project—from technical configuration and production through commissioning and after-sales support.

The goal is not necessarily to find the cheapest manufacturer. It is to find one whose equipment and support model fit the project.


Why Do Global Buyers Source DC Fast Chargers from China?

China's EV supply chain gives buyers access to a wide range of charger architectures, power levels and customization options.

Depending on the manufacturer, buyers can source compact DC wallboxes, conventional integrated chargers, high-power all-in-one chargers and large distributed charging systems.

OEM and ODM options are also relatively common among Chinese suppliers, which can be useful for distributors and project developers building products for specific markets.

However, capabilities vary considerably between manufacturers. Buyers should still verify the exact product, certification, software and support requirements before making a final decision.


Which DC Fast Charger Manufacturer Should You Choose?

There is no single DC fast charger manufacturer that is the right choice for every project.

A public charging operator may prioritize uptime and backend integration. A distributor may care more about certification and customization. A fleet project may place greater weight on power distribution and scalability.

Start with your own requirements:

Market → Power → Connector → Certification → Software → Quantity → Customization → Service

Then compare manufacturers against the same criteria.
